title: Hong Kong's Financial Evolution
text:
Hong Kong's Financial Evolution

China's Bid to Shape Global Capital Flows

Read the full report.

Executive SummaryFor five years, the dominant Western story about Hong Kong has been one of decline. Political autonomy has narrowed. International confidence has been damaged. Singapore has gained ground. The city is increasingly treated as a diminished version of the financial center it once was.This report argues that this diagnosis misses the more consequential transformation underway. Beijing is not simply managing the erosion of a Western-style financial center. It is repurposing Hong Kong into the offshore financial platform of a still-controlled Chinese system, a place where China can obtain many of the benefits of financial openness without surrendering sovereign control over its capital account, the rules governing financial flows into and out of the mainland.Its defining mechanism is easy to misunderstand. Beijing is not opening a route through Hong Kong for Chinese wealth to disperse freely into global markets. Mainland capital moving south remains anchored in Hong Kong through closed-loop channels known collectively as Connect, whose eligible assets, settlement, and use of proceeds Beijing can supervise. What that anchored capital helps create is a deeper offshore financial ecosystem: liquidity, intermediaries, renminbi funding, internationally credible markets, and alternative settlement capacity. It is that financial reach, not unrestricted flow of Chinese savings, that Beijing seeks to project outward.Hong Kong is indispensable because it supplies what the mainland cannot. It offers an internationally legible market, a common-law jurisdiction, convertible currency, global banks, foreign investors, and financial infrastructure that counterparties trust while remaining inside China’s sovereign perimeter. That combination is the strategic asset.The evidence assembled in this report shows that Beijing has already built much of the machinery required to make the model work. What remains unresolved is whether that machinery can reach sufficient scale, and attract enough independent foreign demand, to erode American financial leverage without forcing China to liberalize on Western terms.A financial system built around controlThe transformation rests on four mutually reinforcing functions: savings, credit, equity, and settlement.FIRST FUNCTION: SAVINGSAs more mainland savings accumulate in Hong Kong through these channels, they deepen the city’s liquidity, strengthen its financial intermediaries, and expand the offshore market Beijing wants Hong Kong to anchor. The larger those flows become, the more consequential Hong Kong’s role in China’s financial system becomes.A mainland investor can buy eligible Hong Kong assets, but the capital remains inside a closed loop. The assets that can be purchased are defined, settlement runs through designated infrastructure, currency conversion occurs inside the system rather than in an investor-controlled offshore account, and proceeds return through the same channel.China’s saver gains offshore exposure without gaining unrestricted command over offshore money. That is controlled openness in its purest form.The result is a growing pool of mainland capital inside Hong Kong’s financial system, large enough to deepen liquidity and strengthen the city’s role as an offshore financial center, but without opening the mainland capital account itself.SECOND FUNCTION: CREDITHong Kong has long been the world’s principal offshore center for the renminbi, or RMB, China’s currency. Over the past five years, that role has been materially deepened and broadened, with growth in RMB deposits, bond issuance, bank lending, liquidity facilities, collateral infrastructure, and clearing capacity. Beijing and the Hong Kong authorities have expanded what was already the leading offshore RMB hub into a more complete offshore funding market.The market is still much more Chinese than global. Most offshore RMB issuance remains Chinese or China-linked. Genuine foreign borrowers have appeared, including sovereign and quasi-sovereign issuers from outside China, but they remain limited and concentrated close to China’s economic orbit. Where investor allocation is visible, it looks concentrated in China and the wider region; who ultimately holds that exposure is harder to establish, and that disclosure gap is a genuine limit on what can be verified, not evidence of foreign disengagement.That distinction matters because Beijing does not need the renminbi to replace the dollar globally. A system capable of financing more trade, borrowing, and investment within China’s immediate economic orbit would already reduce dependence on American financial infrastructure and potentially weaken the reach of American financial power.THIRD FUNCTION: EQUITYHong Kong has become the dominant offshore venue for Chinese companies raising international equity capital, and this is where Beijing’s model has advanced furthest. The current shift is no longer mainly a defensive “homecoming” by firms adding Hong Kong listings because of pressure on their US listings. A major part of the newer wave consists of mainland companies already listed in Shanghai or Shenzhen adding a second line of shares in Hong Kong to reach foreign currency and international investors.Mainland institutions now shape the listing pipeline and provide a growing share of market liquidity. Yet international investors remain important to the largest transactions, global banks continue to play a significant distribution role, and foreign demand helps shape valuations for leading companies. That dependence on international capital is precisely why Hong Kong matters. If Beijing made Hong Kong fully mainland-like, it would undermine the international credibility that gives the venue strategic value.The equity market therefore shows controlled openness at its most successful: sovereign influence over the gateway combined with enough genuine openness inside the gateway to keep foreign capital engaged.FOURTH FUNCTION: SETTLEMENTChina has spent a decade building payment and settlement infrastructure that reduces reliance on the dollar correspondent-banking and SWIFT system through which much of US financial leverage is exercised. Hong Kong now sits at the center of that effort, as a major offshore node for renminbi clearing, an access point for cross-border digital-yuan settlement, a participant in mBridge, and a testing ground for tokenized bonds, deposits, and regulated stablecoins.Hong Kong again plays the same role. It supplies the internationally trusted venue, including the legal framework, custody, banking access, and issuance infrastructure. Beijing retains control over the currency crossing the mainland boundary and increasingly over the data architecture through which those transactions move.The newer systems remain far from replacing dollar settlement. Much of the activity is still China-linked, and genuine third-party use remains limited. Replacement is the wrong benchmark.The strategic question is whether Beijing can steadily reduce the number of functions for which dollar access remains the only viable option.THE PARADOX AT THE COREThe entire strategy rests on a contradiction. Hong Kong can perform this role only because its own currency remains tied to the US dollar through a currency-board system that keeps the Hong Kong dollar within a narrow, fixed band against it. That dollar peg gives Hong Kong a freely convertible currency anchor, deep access to dollar liquidity, and the credibility international investors still require. The renminbi cannot yet provide those functions at comparable scale. Beijing therefore has strong reasons to preserve the peg even while building around it.The consequence is a financial system whose dollar foundation remains intact while the activity layered above it becomes progressively more multicurrency and more renminbi-capable. That leaves US leverage over Hong Kong real, though potentially less comprehensive over time. Washington’s leverage comes not from owning Hong Kong’s payment systems, but from the dependence of Hong Kong’s banks and financial institutions on access to the wider dollar-clearing network that makes locally held dollars globally usable. That leverage remains powerful. But its reach could diminish as more financial functions become possible without dollar access.THE WORLD IS USING HONG KONG, SELECTIVELYBeijing can build infrastructure. It cannot manufacture independent demand. That is the most important constraint exposed by this report. On external measures, Hong Kong remains a leading global financial center. Its rankings, IPO activity, wealth-management franchise, and continued presence of global financial institutions do not support a story of terminal decline.But the source of that strength is changing. Non-Chinese borrowers have used Hong Kong’s offshore infrastructure to reach Chinese and Asian liquidity, but only selectively. Sovereign and institutional investors provide much weaker evidence that they actively prefer Hong Kong as the route through which to obtain Chinese exposure. Global banks and asset managers are not leaving, but the business showing the clearest momentum is increasingly tied to Chinese clients, Chinese issuers, renminbi services, and cross-border wealth.That is both the achievement and the limit of Beijing’s strategy so far: the machinery works, money flows and the venue remains credible, but much of the traction still depends on China’s own economic weight rather than autonomous foreign demand. The equity market, where genuine international investor demand is clearest, remains an important exception.Four futuresThe next five years will test whether that balance can persist. This report ranks four plausible paths.Managed expansion is the most likely. Beijing continues widening and deepening Hong Kong’s role while keeping the mainland capital account controlled. More activity migrates onto renminbi and Chinese financial rails, but independent foreign demand grows only slowly.Disruption ranks second. A mainland economic crisis, geopolitical rupture, sanctions shock, or severe Hong Kong stress forces Beijing to change course abruptly.An inward turn ranks third. Beijing prioritizes domestic financing and onshore markets, starving Hong Kong of some of the capital and activity needed to deepen its offshore role.Western-style opening is the least likely. China moves toward much fuller capital-account liberalization, turning Hong Kong into part of a genuinely open Chinese financial system rather than the controlled offshore interface described in this report.The more activity that migrates onto yuan and Chinese payment rails without requiring full capital-account liberalization or broad foreign conviction, the stronger the evidence that this third model can work on its own terms.What Washington should do differentlyThe implications for the United States follow directly. Washington should avoid treating Hong Kong as a fading asset or assuming the answer is to spend its remaining leverage as aggressively as possible before that leverage decays. Both responses misread the problem.American power rests not only on the ability to deny access to the dollar system, but on the fact that the dollar system remains the most useful, liquid, trusted, and efficient financial network in the world.First, the United States should strengthen the dollar’s competitive position. Treasury and the Federal Reserve should treat wholesale tokenized settlement, using digital representations of central-bank and commercial-bank money to settle large financial transactions more efficiently, as a strategic priority, and support deeper Asian dollar-clearing capacity in Tokyo, Singapore, and Manila.Second, leverage should remain targeted rather than systemic. Congress should resist conditioning Hong Kong’s entire dollar-clearing relationship on sanctions compliance. Entity-specific enforcement under existing authorities is more likely to change institutional behavior without accelerating the migration of the wider system away from dollar rails.Third, Washington should assess spillovers before acting. Sanctions or export-control measures likely to affect Chinese or Hong Kong financial institutions should be tested not only for their direct effectiveness but for their impact on allied institutions, financial stability, retaliation risk, and incentives to develop alternatives to the dollar.Fourth, allied coordination should take place before a crisis, not during one. The United Kingdom is particularly exposed through its banking system, while Singapore, Japan, the Philippines, Gulf states, and Southeast Asian partners matter to the broader task of building resilient dollar infrastructure.Fifth, Washington should prepare specifically for a Taiwan contingency. It needs a standing, regularly updated assessment of what Hong Kong-related dollar leverage would still achieve in a crisis, what collateral damage its use would impose, and what alternatives Beijing would have available by then.Together, these recommendations form a single strategy. Dollar leverage is a valuable asset whose reach could diminish over time, and preserving it depends on investing in the system that makes it possible. The US needs to do both at once: calibrate its use of leverage so it doesn’t provoke faster migration away from dollar rails, and invest in the dollar system’s competitiveness so restraint doesn’t just manage a slow decline.The bottom lineThat combination may ultimately prove unstable. Foreign demand may never deepen enough. The renminbi may remain too constrained. Beijing may tighten the system whenever genuine openness threatens control. The dollar peg may remain indispensable for longer than Beijing would like. But those are limits to a strategy that already exists, not evidence that no strategy exists.Beijing has stated its intent, built much of the infrastructure required to pursue it, and begun shifting financial activity onto systems that reduce dependence on American-controlled rails. The United States does not need to guess at Beijing’s direction or wait for success to become undeniable before responding. It needs the imagination and discipline to ask the right questions and read the evidence already in front of it, and the will to compete on the strength of America’s own financial system rather than on the hope that China’s model falls short.
